A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Metis by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2 FP8/FP4 training experiments, GLUE results, component ablations, and spectral analyses, including an appendix analysis.

after.justification: v4 reports original simulated FP4 training experiments on GPT-2 and LLaMA-3, downstream evaluations, comparator experiments, ablations, and additional spectral and sampling analyses.

M1.justification: v4 retains low-rank-plus-residual quantization but adds dynamic activation decomposition and sparse sequence sampling before randomized decomposition. v1 directly quantizes activations in its forward equations. Its adaptive spectral learning rate and dual-range regularization components are absent from v4's proposed framework and ablations.

E1.justification: DCLM pretraining remains, but the six GLUE evaluation tasks are replaced by ARC-Challenge/Easy, BoolQ, LAMBADA, PIQA, RACE, and HellaSwag. This substantially changes downstream coverage toward question answering, commonsense reasoning, and cloze prediction.

E2.justification: v4 adds the authors' implementation of NVIDIA's FP4 training recipe, using Hadamard transforms and stochastic rounding, in GPT-2 performance comparisons and spectral diagnostics. Direct NVFP4 remains a comparator; v1's direct FP8E4M3 and MXFP4 comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: v4 adds LLaMA-3 8B to training-performance comparisons and specifies 100B training tokens per model, versus approximately 88B for v1's 1.1B FP4 model and subsets otherwise. Controls change from FP32 to BF16, and the stated FP4 decomposition rank changes from 50% in v1 Section 4.1 to 1.5% in v4 Section 4.

E4.justification: Decomposition ablations are revised to distinguish weights, activations, and gradients, and a full-batch-versus-sparse-sampling control is added. Adaptive-rate and regularizer ablations disappear. v4 adds rank sensitivity, sampling/subspace alignment, Hadamard comparison diagnostics, and broader layer/module analyses; v1's gradient-update alignment analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies training seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v4 Figures 4 and 25 introduce shaded bands around sampling-alignment curves, but neither captions nor text defines them. Whether these constitute statistical uncertainty reporting cannot be established.

E6.justification: Large portions of the results are replaced. For GPT-2 1.1B, v1 Table 3 reports Metis-NVFP4 loss 3.36 versus FP32's 3.29; v4 Table 1 reports 3.01 versus BF16's 3.09 under changed settings, so these are not matched-setting gains. v4 adds LLaMA-3 results, NVIDIA-recipe comparisons, and sensitivity findings, while removing FP8/MXFP4/GLUE results. The public-model elbow fractions are retained in v4 Figure 7.

T1.justification: v4 removes v1's gradient-singular perturbation derivation and variance/Popoviciu range argument. It adds probabilistic covariance-concentration and eigengap-based subspace-preservation arguments using matrix Chernoff, Davis–Kahan, and randomized-SVD results. Computational complexity is also rederived to include sampled activation and gradient decomposition.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a three-component FP8/FP4 framework claiming FP8 parity or superiority to FP32 toward scalable FP4 spectral preservation. v4 foregrounds sparse sampling, near-BF16 performance on LLaMA-3 8B, and superiority to the authors' NVIDIA-recipe implementation. The FP8 and adaptive-rate/regularization contribution claims disappear.

C2.justification: v4 adds reduced interference between low-rank and residual branches as an explanation for GPT-2 gains and changes the appendix isotropy interpretation from singular factors to the residual branch. It explicitly states that simulated execution prevents measuring native runtime and memory benefits and qualifies the NVIDIA comparison as an unofficial implementation. v1's gradient-growth and adaptive-update interpretations are removed.

D1.justification: v4 adds data segmentation/filtering instructions, Qwen3-based perplexity filtering, default stochastic rounding, and explicit FP4 value-set and BF16-accumulation documentation. However, v1's optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch/sequence sizes, clipping, H100 hardware, and PyTorch/CUDA details disappear. The code pointer changes from GitHub to an anonymized repository; access was not externally verified.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantial grounding in randomized SVD, matrix concentration, and eigenspace perturbation literature, alongside FP8-training and new dataset/model references. NVIDIA's FP4 training recipe becomes a prominent competing approach. The existing three-family outlier-mitigation taxonomy and most associated methods remain, with their discussion condensed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, analysis, and methods are extensively rewritten around FP4. Efficiency analysis moves into the method section, experiments are reorganized into main results, ablations, and extended evaluation, and appendices are organized into analysis, method, and experimental support. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v4 adds an overview figure, redraws training curves with stacked panels and zoomed insets, consolidates performance tables, and introduces extensive appendix plots. v1 Figure 1 is relocated and reformatted as v4 Figure 7. v1 Figure 8(a) appears to reappear as v4 Figure 27 with different tensor labels, while its companion histogram is omitted.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens evaluation beyond v1's GPT-2 training comparisons through LLaMA-3 8B, a relevant NVIDIA-recipe comparator, and targeted sampling/rank tests. However, it removes important training details, reports inconsistent Metis downstream scores between Tables 1 and 2, and apparently reuses v1 Figure 8(a) with a different tensor interpretation in Figure 27. These unresolved reproducibility and result-attribution issues prevent a confident judgment of net quality improvement.
